extracted.intended_audience: recipients of federal education funds (schools and colleges), school administrators, legal counsel, policymakers, and Title IX commenters/advocates
extracted.subtask_description: Explanation and defense of the Department of Education's final rule §106.10 clarifying that Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination encompasses sexual orientation, gender identity, and sex characteristics, including discussion of statutory authority, judicial precedent, preemption, exceptions, and enforcement approach.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delegated authority to promulgate §106.10
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has delegated authority under Title IX (20 U.S.C. 1682) and other statutes to promulgate regulations implementing Title IX, including §106.10.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble relies on the statutory grant that federal agencies administering education funding establish requirements to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate and enforce them by any means authorized by law (including termination of funding). Cited authority includes 20 U.S.C. 1682 and Supreme Court precedent (e.g., Gebser).

rubrics_metrics.name: Coverage of sexual orientation and gender identity under Title IX
rubrics_metrics.description: §106.10 covers discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity as forms of sex discrimination under Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department finds this coverage consistent with Supreme Court and federal court holdings (e.g., Bostock; Grabowski; Grimm) and thus properly promulgated to effectuate Title IX's nondiscrimination mandate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Federal preemption of conflicting State laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients' obligation to comply with Title IX and these final regulations is not obviated by State or local laws that conflict with Title IX.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: State laws can be preempted when it is impossible to comply with both federal and state requirements or when state law obstructs Congress's purposes. Cited cases include Freightliner Corp., Hillsborough County, and others. If State laws do not conflict, recipients should be able to comply with both.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulations do not commandeer State/local education policy or curriculum
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not prevent States or local governments from adopting innovative, customized approaches to education, nor do they dictate curriculum.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: 34 CFR 106.42 states nothing in the Title IX regulations requires or prohibits use of particular textbooks or curricular materials. The Department declines to opine on specific State laws or policies without fact-specific evaluation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limits of Department of Education Organization Act authority
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations do not grant the Department authority to direct, supervise, or control the administration or personnel of any recipient.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This limitation is consistent with 20 U.S.C. 3403(b) and is cited to rebut claims that the Department exceeded its authority under the Organization Act.

rubrics_metrics.name: Compliance with APA notice-and-comment rulemaking
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has complied with all applicable Administrative Procedure Act (APA) requirements for this rulemaking.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Although a district court issued a preliminary injunction related to a different Bostock NOI, the Department contends that that holding does not affect the Department's statutory authority for the final regulations. Cases concerning notice-and-comment (e.g., Mann) do not alter the Department's position because the Department followed the APA for this rulemaking.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of Title VII/Bostock reasoning to inform Title IX interpretation
rubrics_metrics.description: Federal courts commonly look to Title VII jurisprudence, including Bostock, to inform the interpretation of Title IX's prohibition on sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department reasons that phrases like 'because of' and 'on the basis of' have been used interchangeably by the Supreme Court (including in Bostock), and multiple courts of appeals have read Title IX similarly to Title VII. The preamble cites cases and explains why Title VII reasoning appropriately informs Title IX interpretation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation standards (but-for and motivating-factor) encompass SOGI discrimination
rubrics_metrics.description: Both the but-for causation standard and the more forgiving motivating-factor standard can encompass discrimination on the basis of sexual orientation and gender identity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Bostock's analysis and subsequent circuit decisions show that liability can follow under a motivating-factor test and that even the but-for standard can capture SOGI-related discrimination. The Department cites cases (e.g., Doe v. William Marsh Rice Univ.) to support this point.

rubrics_metrics.name: No regulatory definition required for 'gender identity' or 'sexual orientation'
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to define 'gender identity' or 'sexual orientation' in the Title IX regulations because courts and other laws routinely use and interpret these terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The preamble cites numerous cases (Bostock; Whitaker; Grimm; Grabowski; Hively) demonstrating widespread judicial usage. The Department notes that subjectivity or private knowledge of another's identity does not undermine its status as a protected basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Gender identity encompasses transgender status
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department determined that 'gender identity' includes a person's transgender status but is a broader term that more fully reflects Title IX's protections.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department declines to substitute 'transgender status' for 'gender identity,' noting Bostock's instruction that discrimination because of inconsistent gender identity implicates sex and citing cases supporting inclusion of transgender individuals.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sex characteristics are protected (physiological traits, including intersex)
rubrics_metrics.description: The term 'sex characteristics' is intended to refer to physiological, sex-based characteristics (anatomy, hormones, chromosomes) and includes intersex traits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department agrees this protection is consistent with Title IX and court precedent (e.g., Bostock, Grimm) and rejects the view that protection should be limited to reproductive capacity or require medical diagnosis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Permissible sex separation is limited and cannot be based on sexual orientation
rubrics_metrics.description: When the regulations permit separation based on sex, that allowance does not extend to separation based on sexual orientation or other bases in §106.10; intentional separation by sexual orientation generally constitutes sex discrimination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department explains that §106.10 does not permit recipients to separate students on the basis of sexual orientation and cites Bostock as relevant authority.

rubrics_metrics.name: First Amendment and religious-exemption protections maintained
rubrics_metrics.description: Recipients' compliance with the final regulations must be carried out consistent with First Amendment protections and Title IX's religious exemption.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department references §106.6(d) and 20 U.S.C. 1681(a)(3), emphasizing that nothing in the regulations requires restriction of rights protected under the First Amendment or other constitutional provisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enforcement approach is fact-specific; Department will investigate complaints
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department declines to provide prescriptive definitions or specific examples of conduct that constitute SOGI discrimination in the regulations, because determinations depend on fact-specific investigations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department will investigate complaints and make fact-specific determinations (citing 34 CFR 100.7 and incorporation through 34 CFR 106.81), rather than issuing general opinions about how the regulations apply to specific policies or laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Recipients retain discretion to shape nondiscriminatory responses
rubrics_metrics.description: The final regulations clarify legal obligations but do not prescribe specific outcomes; recipients have discretion to shape responses to sex discrimination in nondiscriminatory ways that account for parties' needs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department emphasizes that the regulations clarify scope but that outcomes will turn on particular facts and circumstances; this preserves recipient flexibility within nondiscrimination requirements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Regulatory impact: clarification expected to increase nondiscrimination protections
rubrics_metrics.description: The Department has examined relevant data and concluded that clarifying Title IX's scope will result in greater nondiscrimination protection and increased access to education for affected students and employees.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For detailed cost-benefit analysis, the preamble points to the Regulatory Impact Analysis; the Department sees net benefits in clarifying protections for LGBTQI+ students and employees.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential overlap with ADA obligations for gender dysphoria
rubrics_metrics.description: Title IX coverage of gender identity may overlap with Americans with Disabilities Act obligations where courts have treated gender dysphoria as a disability, creating potentially overlapping obligations for recipients.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Department notes Fourth Circuit recognition that ADA protections can apply to transgender people suffering from gender dysphoria and that recipients may have overlapping duties under both statutes (citing Williams v. Kincaid).
